hero.name: Naveen
hero.who: a 39-year-old sweet shop owner in Varanasi whose every disagreement becomes a fight

story.b: Naveen and his elder brother Mukesh run the sweet shop their father opened near Godowlia in Varanasi. They argue about almost everything. A new freezer, the price of kaju katli, who handles the five o'clock milk delivery, whether to open a second counter. Every argument ends the same way. One brother wins, the other sulks for days, and the staff tiptoe around them. Their wives no longer come to the shop together. One night, after a shouting match about the freezer, Naveen sits alone on the ghat steps with a kulhad of chai. He realises the two of them have not agreed on anything calmly in two years, and the shop is starting to feel it.

ask.q: Every disagreement with his brother ends with a winner and a sulker. What should Naveen change first?
o: Prepare better arguments, so he wins more often
Give in every time, so at least there is peace
Look for ways they both get a fair deal and stay close
ask.why: Winning more leaves his brother sulking, and giving in every time leaves Naveen bitter, so the fights only change shape. Searching for an outcome that is fair to both protects the shop and the relationship at the same time.

chapters.take: A good agreement is one where nobody has to be the loser.

story.b: The freezer fight returns on Monday. The old one breaks down every few weeks, and trays of rasmalai have spoiled twice this month. Mukesh says Naveen always wants to waste money. Naveen feels the old heat and almost replies that Mukesh is a miser. Instead he fetches the shop register and the repair bills and lays them on the counter. He pulls up a second stool so they sit side by side, facing the pages. This is our problem, he says, not yours or mine. Mukesh grumbles but leans in. Together they add up what the repairs and spoiled sweets have cost. For the first time in weeks, they are looking at the same thing.

ask.q: Mukesh says Naveen always wastes money. What is Naveen's best response?
o: Point out the times Mukesh wasted money too, to even things out
Let the remark pass and bring them both back to the freezer problem
Walk out, since nothing useful can happen while Mukesh insults him
ask.why: Firing back turns a freezer problem into a fight about who is worse. Walking out leaves the problem sitting there. Staying kind to his brother while putting the actual issue on the table lets them face it together, side by side.

chapters.take: Be soft on the person and clear on the problem.

story.b: Next comes closing time. Mukesh insists the shop must stay open till eleven at night. Naveen wants to close at nine, because his daughter has board exams and he never eats dinner with her. They have fought about this for months. This time Naveen asks a question instead. Why does eleven matter so much? Mukesh says the late crowd coming back from the ghats buys the most. Naveen asks again, gently, why that matters so much right now. Mukesh admits he is scared the new shop down the lane will steal those customers. Suddenly Naveen understands. Mukesh does not care about the clock. He cares about the shop surviving. And Naveen cares about dinner, not the clock either.

ask.q: Mukesh insists on staying open till eleven. What should Naveen do first?
o: Ask gently why the late hours matter so much to him
Insist on nine, since he has a family to think of too
Agree on ten, splitting the difference to end the fight
ask.why: Insisting on nine just meets one position with another. Splitting the difference sounds fair but may satisfy neither real need. Asking why uncovers what Mukesh truly cares about, and once both interests are clear, better answers start to appear.

chapters.take: Ask why someone wants something. The why opens new doors.

story.b: After closing one night, the brothers sit with two kulhads of chai and a school notebook. Naveen suggests a rule. For ten minutes they will list every possible answer to the closing time problem, and nobody is allowed to say that will not work. The first idea is hiring a helper for late evenings. Then the ideas keep coming. Take turns by week. Naveen opens early, Mukesh closes late. Stay open late only on weekends. Sell boxed sweets through a delivery app after nine. Train their cousin Raju. Only when the page is full do they start choosing. In the end they combine three ideas, and both of them walk home smiling.

ask.q: They have their first idea, a helper for late evenings. What should they do next?
o: Pick it straight away, since a decent answer is enough
Keep listing more options before judging any of them
Debate the helper idea until one of them agrees to it
ask.why: Grabbing the first answer, or arguing over one idea, shrinks the choice back into a tug of war. Listing many options first, without judging, raises the chance of finding one that gives both brothers something they really value.

chapters.take: Invent many options before you choose one.

story.b: Cashew prices have shot up, and the brothers disagree about the kaju katli. Mukesh wants a big price jump. Naveen fears losing loyal customers. In the past, whoever shouted longer would have won. This time Naveen suggests they let something outside both of them decide. They pull out the wholesaler bills for cashew, sugar and ghee from the last three months. They walk around the market and note what three well-known shops charge for similar quality. Then they sit down with the numbers. The fair price turns out to be in between, a little closer to Mukesh's figure. Naveen agrees easily. He is not giving in to his brother. He is following the numbers.

ask.q: The brothers disagree about raising the kaju katli price. What is the fairest way to settle it?
o: Let the elder brother decide, since that is the family tradition
Keep arguing until one of them gets tired and gives in
Use ingredient costs and nearby shops' prices as a shared guide
ask.why: Deciding by age or by stamina leaves one side feeling beaten, and resentment builds. An outside standard, like actual costs and what similar shops charge, gives both a fair reference. Nobody gives in to the other; they both follow something fair.

chapters.take: When wills clash, agree on a fair outside standard instead.

story.b: A big wedding caterer comes to the shop with an offer. Fifty kilos of laddoos every month, but at a price far below their usual rate, and he wants an answer today. Naveen feels the pressure. A big order sounds wonderful. Before replying, he steps into the back room and writes one question in the notebook. What will we do if this deal does not happen? The answer is clear. Wedding season is coming, and their regular orders already fill most of the kitchen, at better rates. With that written down, Naveen feels calm. He goes back and politely asks for a fairer price. The caterer frowns, then raises his offer.

ask.q: The caterer pushes Naveen to accept a low price today. What should Naveen do before replying?
o: Get clear on what the shop will do if this deal falls through
Accept quickly, since a big order may never come again
Refuse angrily, to show the caterer he cannot be pushed
ask.why: Knowing his fallback, steady regular orders at better rates, tells Naveen how good this deal must be to beat it. Accepting out of fear can lock the shop into a loss, and an angry no wastes a deal that might become fair. A clear walk-away option keeps him calm.

chapters.take: Know your walk-away option, and you will not take a bad deal out of fear.

story.b: A few months later, the shop has a new rhythm. Naveen opens at seven and leaves at eight to eat dinner with his daughter, who is studying for her boards. Mukesh arrives late morning and closes at eleven, happy with the late crowd. A helper covers weekends. The new freezer hums in the corner, and no rasmalai has spoiled since. The caterer's order runs at a fair price. The brothers still disagree, often. But now they reach for the notebook and a kulhad of chai instead of raising their voices. Their wives came to the shop together during the festival rush. At home, when his daughter asks for a later curfew, Naveen catches himself and asks why.

chapters.take: Face the problem together, and fights turn into fair deals.
